newsitem.title: UK: British Airways says looking at French Air Liberte.
newsitem.headline: British Airways says looking at French Air Liberte.

text.p: British Airways Plc said on Friday that its French associate airline TAT had been in contact with the adminstrators of France's Air Liberte to assess parts of the troubled airline for possible purchase.
Michael Blunt, BA's public relations manager, said: "TAT has been in contact with the administrator to assess what he is looking to realise out of the remaining assets of Air Liberte."
In Paris, the daily newspaper Le Monde reported that TAT expected to make an offfer for Air Liberte "in the next few days" but Blunt said he was not aware of any urgency.
"There is no indication of any timetable as yet on this -- it's early days," he told Reuters by telephone.
Privately-owned Air Liberte was put into legal adminstration on September 26 after defaulting on payments.

Airline industry sources said that TAT was racing with AOM, part of the troubled bank group Credit Lyonnais, which has also been looking to a possible deal with Air Liberte. Le Monde said that BA's British arch-rival Virgin was also in the frame.

According to the newspaper, Virgin, which owns long-haul carrier Virgin Atlantic Airways and recently started up Brussels-based European regional airline Virgin Express, "is equally ready to make an offer to take over Air Liberte".

Le Monde also said the French authorities were not happy with the British interest in Air Liberte and would prefer a domestic group formed that linked AOM, Air Liberte and Euralair, to create a second French-owned player alongside Air France.
Blunt said that, in TAT's view, it had to examine the possibility that Air Liberte might enable it to compete better in France with Air Inter Europe, part of the Air France group.
Meanwhile, Air Liberte has begun a rescue plan that involves taking several large planes out of its fleet and cutting routes -- both long-haul to Africa and Canada and some internal ones.
The plan, under which it is cutting 285 jobs and focusing on medium- and short-haul flights, is to run for about six months.
